title: Taking the Twinkle Out of the Stars

passage.title: Taking the Twinkle Out of the Stars
passage.author: BEACON Assessment Lab
passage.text:
To a camper looking up at the night sky, a twinkling star is a lovely sight. To a scientist at a giant mountain scope, though, that same twinkle is a major problem. Stars do not flicker out in deep space. Their light travels in steady, straight beams across trillions of miles of empty vacuum. The trouble starts only during the last split second. That is when starlight plunges into Earth's restless blanket of air.

High above the ground, winds churn warm and cool pockets of air into a turbulent sea. Cold air is denser than warm air. Each moving pocket bends passing starlight in a slightly new way. By the time a beam of starlight hits a mirror on a peak, it has been jiggled dozens of times. This fast bending makes distant stars and worlds dance and blur into fuzzy blobs. It is much like trying to read a coin lying at the bottom of a rippling swimming pool.

For decades, the only way to escape this air blur was to launch expensive telescopes into orbit above the sky. Then engineers built a smart system called adaptive optics. First, the dome crew shines a bright yellow laser beam straight up into the night sky. High in the upper air, the laser makes a layer of sodium atoms glow like an artificial guide star. Because the computer knows the exact shape a pinpoint star should have, it can measure precisely how the shifting wind pockets distort that glowing spot.

Next, the system sends fast signals to a thin, bendable glass mirror inside the scope. Incoming starlight from distant galaxies, bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air, is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror. Hundreds of these tiny rods push and pull the glass up to a thousand times each second. Each small bend cancels out the exact ripple in the air above.

With adaptive optics turned on, a blurry blob on the screen snaps into a sharp image in the blink of an eye. Ground scopes can now spot faint moons around far worlds. They can even watch stars swirl around the heart of our galaxy. By learning to compensate for shifting air in real time, astronomers have given Earthbound telescopes a view almost as clear as space itself.

tier2Words.definition: Moving in a rough, swirling, and unsteady way
tier2Words.contextClue: High winds 'churn warm and cool pockets of air' that jiggle passing starlight.

tier2Words.definition: To become unclear, smeared, or fuzzy in outline
tier2Words.rootHint: Middle English bleren (to dim or make indistinct)
tier2Words.contextClue: Paired with 'dance and blur into fuzzy blobs' like looking through a rippling pool.

tier2Words.definition: To twist or bend something out of its true, normal shape
tier2Words.contextClue: Echoed in Paragraph 4 as 'bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air.'

tier2Words.definition: To make up for or cancel out an unwanted effect
tier2Words.rootHint: com- + pensare (Latin root meaning 'to weigh or balance against')
tier2Words.contextClue: In Paragraph 4, 'Each small bend cancels out the exact ripple in the air above.'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Incoming starlight from distant galaxies, bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air, is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror."

In the main clause of this sentence, what sharpens the incoming starlight?

options.text: Swirling pockets of warm and cool air high in the sky
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the agent inside the middle participial phrase ('bent out of shape by swirling pockets...') with the agent that sharpens the starlight.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the noun inside the middle describing phrase ('bent out of shape by swirling pockets...') with what actually sharpens the starlight.

options.text: Distant galaxies shining across trillions of miles
options.diagnosticNote: Selects the object of the preposition 'from distant galaxies' rather than the mechanism that sharpens the light.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice selects the noun after 'from distant galaxies' rather than the mechanism that sharpens the light.

options.text: Tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror
options.diagnosticNote: Correctly identifies the passive agent following the main verb ('is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror').
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror').

options.text: Incoming starlight plunging into Earth's atmosphere
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the grammatical subject/receiver ('Incoming starlight') with the actor performing the sharpening.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the subject receiving the action ('Incoming starlight') with the actor performing the sharpening.

questions.provingSentenceText: Incoming starlight from distant galaxies, bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air, is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer correctly identifies the doer of the action following the main verb ('is instantly sharpened by tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror').
questions.parentExplanation: Sentence Surgery (ELAGSE5L1) with a double-'by' passive trap. Swirling pockets of air bent the light out of shape, whereas 'tiny pistons pushing behind the flexible glass mirror' sharpened it.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 4, watch out for two 'by' phrases! Find the main verb 'is instantly sharpened by' to see what fixes the light.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Because the computer knows the exact shape a pinpoint star should have, it can measure precisely how the shifting wind pockets distort that glowing spot."

What does the word distort mean as it is used in the sentence?

options.text: Keep completely still and razor-sharp
options.diagnosticNote: Reverses the effect of the wind pockets; the shifting air blurs and bends the light, while the mirror makes it sharp.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice reverses the effect of the wind pockets; the shifting air blurs and bends the light, while the mirror makes it sharp.

options.text: Bend or twist out of its true shape
options.diagnosticNote: Matches the Latin root 'tort' (twist) and Paragraph 4's restatement ('bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air').
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer matches the Latin root 'tort' (twist) and Paragraph 4's restatement ('bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air').

options.text: Launch high into orbit above the clouds
options.diagnosticNote: Borrows the idea of launching space telescopes from earlier in Paragraph 3.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice borrows the idea of launching space telescopes from earlier in Paragraph 3.

options.text: Cool down the temperature of the upper sky
options.diagnosticNote: Misinterprets the optical measurement of light shape as changing air temperature.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice misinterprets the optical measurement of light shape as changing air temperature.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because the computer knows the exact shape a pinpoint star should have, it can measure precisely how the shifting wind pockets distort that glowing spot.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer matches the Latin root 'tort' (twist) and Paragraph 4's restatement ('bent out of shape by swirling pockets of warm and cool air').
questions.parentExplanation: Vocabulary in Context (ELAGSE5RI4). Paragraph 2 ('bends passing starlight... into fuzzy blobs') and Paragraph 4 ('bent out of shape') confirm that 'distort' means to twist or bend out of shape.
questions.retryHint: Check the next paragraph for a clue: what do the swirling pockets of air do to the shape of incoming starlight?

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why does an adaptive optics observatory shine a yellow laser beam high into the night sky?

options.text: The laser creates a glowing artificial guide star so the computer can measure how wind pockets are bending light at that moment.
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately traces the function of the laser guide star explained in Paragraph 3.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer accurately traces the function of the laser guide star explained in Paragraph 3.

options.text: The hot laser beam heats up the cold pockets of air until the wind stops blowing above the mountain.
options.diagnosticNote: Invents the idea that the laser heats the sky to stop the wind, rather than creating a reference spot of light.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice invents the idea that the laser heats the sky to stop the wind, rather than creating a reference spot of light.

options.text: The yellow beam bounces off moons in distant galaxies and brings photographs back to the screen.
options.diagnosticNote: Confuses the upper-atmosphere sodium layer with distant galaxies trillions of miles away.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice confuses the upper-atmosphere sodium layer with distant galaxies trillions of miles away.

options.text: The laser melts the glass mirror inside the telescope so it can bend more easily.
options.diagnosticNote: Misconnects the laser beam in Paragraph 3 with the flexible mirror moved by pistons in Paragraph 4.
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice wrongly connects the laser beam in Paragraph 3 with the flexible mirror moved by pistons in Paragraph 4.

questions.provingSentenceText: High in the upper air, the laser makes a layer of sodium atoms glow like an artificial guide star.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer accurately traces the function of the laser guide star explained in Paragraph 3.
questions.parentExplanation: Click-to-Prove Scientific Process (ELAGSE5RI3). Paragraph 3 explains that the laser excites sodium atoms in the upper atmosphere to create an artificial guide star, giving the computer a reference point to measure air ripples.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 3 for the sentence that tells what the laser creates high in the upper air.

questions.prompt: Why does the author include the comparison to "trying to read a coin lying at the bottom of a rippling swimming pool" at the end of Paragraph 2?

options.text: To explain how astronomers pay for expensive space telescopes using coins collected at observatories
options.diagnosticNote: Latching onto the word 'coin' and connecting it to 'expensive telescopes' in Paragraph 3.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—picking the word 'coin' and connecting it to 'expensive telescopes' in Paragraph 3.

options.text: To prove that Earth's upper atmosphere is filled with liquid water just like a swimming pool
options.diagnosticNote: Takes the figurative analogy literally, confusing air pockets with liquid swimming pool water.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice takes the figurative analogy literally, confusing air pockets with liquid swimming pool water.

options.text: To help the reader picture how moving layers of air bend starlight and make clear objects look wavy and blurred
options.diagnosticNote: Accurately explains how the everyday analogy makes the abstract optical concept of atmospheric refraction concrete for readers.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer accurately explains how the everyday analogy makes the abstract optical concept of atmospheric refraction concrete for readers.

options.text: To show that telescope mirrors must be kept underwater to stay cool at night
options.diagnosticNote: Invents an unsupported claim about underwater telescope mirrors.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice invents an unsupported claim about underwater telescope mirrors.

questions.provingSentenceText: It is much like trying to read a coin lying at the bottom of a rippling swimming pool.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer accurately explains how the everyday analogy makes the abstract optical concept of atmospheric refraction concrete for readers.
questions.parentExplanation: Explanatory Analogy & Craft (ELAGSE5RI5/RI4). The author compares looking at stars through turbulent air pockets to reading a coin through rippling pool water so readers can visualize how clear light gets jiggled into a blurry image.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 2, think about what happens to the look of a coin under rippling water, and compare that to starlight passing through churning air.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Stars do not actually flicker in deep space because their light travels in straight lines across trillions of miles of vacuum.
options.diagnosticNote: States only an introductory background fact from Paragraph 1 rather than the passage's central topic of adaptive optics.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice states only an introductory background fact from Paragraph 1 rather than the passage's central topic of adaptive optics.

options.text: Adaptive optics systems use laser guide stars and fast-bending mirrors to cancel out atmospheric blur, allowing ground telescopes to capture sharp images of space.
options.diagnosticNote: Synthesizes the atmospheric blur problem (Paras 1-2), the laser and flexible mirror mechanism (Paras 3-4), and the resulting clear astronomical views (Para 5).
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This answer brings together the atmospheric blur problem (Paragraphs 1 to 2), the laser and flexible mirror mechanism (Paragraphs 3 to 4), and the resulting clear astronomical views (Paragraph 5).

options.text: Launching telescopes into orbit is the only possible way for astronomers to take clear pictures of distant galaxies.
options.diagnosticNote: Contradicts Paragraphs 3-5, which explain how adaptive optics solved this problem for ground telescopes.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice contradicts Paragraphs 3-5, which explain how adaptive optics solved this problem for ground telescopes.

options.text: Campers enjoy looking at twinkling stars at night, but astronomers dislike going outside in the cold mountain wind.
options.diagnosticNote: Trivializes the opening hook in Paragraph 1 and misses the scientific focus of the text.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this choice oversimplifies the opening hook in Paragraph 1 and misses the scientific focus of the text.

questions.provingSentenceText: By learning to compensate for shifting air in real time, astronomers have given Earthbound telescopes a view almost as clear as space itself.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This answer brings together the atmospheric blur problem (Paragraphs 1 to 2), the laser and flexible mirror mechanism (Paragraphs 3 to 4), and the resulting clear astronomical views (Paragraph 5).
questions.parentExplanation: Focus standard ELAGSE5RI2 (Central Idea). Option B integrates the problem (atmospheric distortion), the engineering solution (laser guide stars + flexible mirrors), and the outcome (space-quality views from Earth).
questions.retryHint: In Paragraphs 1 to 5, choose the summary that covers both the problem of blurry air and how adaptive optics fixes it for ground telescopes.
